speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE RESPECTING RETIREMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext:
I should like to table the correspondence exchanged between the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and myself. In a letter dated October 5 the president, Mr. Ouimet, states that because of certain personal and professional reasons he has come to the conclusion that he should not carry on as head of the corporation after the proposed new legislation comes into effect, which he considers will be early in the new year.
When I received this letter I replied to Mr. Ouimet that in the circumstances outlined in his letter, which is now being tabled, I felt that, on behalf of the government, I would have to accept his decision, which I did with great regret; and I added, in my letter, an expression of gratitude and appreciation for the outstanding contribution Mr. Ouimet has made to the corporation over a long period of years.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE RESPECTING RETIREMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: Is it agreed that the correspondence referred to by the Right Hon. Prime Minister be tabled?

subtopic: TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE RESPECTING RETIREMENT OF PRESIDENT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE RESPECTING RETIREMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext:
I will say at once, as far as the president of the C.B.C. is concerned, that we appointed him when we were in power and that he has served at length in the position to which he was appointed.
However, behind all this there is great uncertainty regarding the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and I feel the committee on broadcasting should be convened at once. We would like to know what is to happen to Captain Briggs. Has the government communicated with him? Has he been informed whether he is to be continued in office beyond the period for which his appointment runs, which I believe is up to the latter part of January, 1967.
We should also like to know the circumstances in which Mr. John Kerr was appointed as supervisor of programs, one of the most sensitive of the senior positions if the C.B.C. is to remain politically unimpaired.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, October 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Sauve for the second reading of Bill No. C-218, to provide assistance to livestock feeders in eastern Canada and British Columbia.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN STORAGE AND TRANSPORTATION COSTS
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN STORAGE AND TRANSPORTATION COSTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take full advantage of this opportunity to make some remarks on the Canadian livestock feed board contemplated under Bill No. C-218.
Because of the importance of the principle of this bill the members of the opposition have followed its development with a great deal of interest. Certainly, on hearing the remarks of the minister, and having had an opportunity of examining them in detail, we can find no quarrel with the object of the bill, which is to rectify an unfortunate condition that has existed in eastern Canada for some years with respect to what was considered by livestock feeders and the producers of feed grains as abnormal profit taking, especially under conditions of short supply or increased transportation cost.
Having said that we have no objection to the principle of the bill, may I take these few moments allocated to me to point out some clauses of the bill which have given me great misgivings.
In developing this bill to correct a grave problem the government has, by the provisions of the bill, projected itself further into free enterprise. That is so because under the

October 7, 1986

Canadian Livestock Feed Board provisions of this bill the committee as set up can have almost unlimited power as far as the flow of feed grains is concerned. Once again this is an attempt to correct the situation in one segment of Canada. As happens in matters of this kind when such corrective measures are taken, something, that can be of benefit to one locality of Canada very often works a hardship to other sections of Canada.
When we look at the principle of this bill and the way in which it is set out, the first thing that comes to mind is the fact that we seem to be working to contrary ends. It is true that we have a grain board in the west that has worked very successfully throughout the years and has been responsible for the continuing high prices received by western producers of feed grains and grains of all kinds. Now, however, under this bill the government proposes to set up a government bureau the principle of which is in effect almost directly contrary to the principle of the wheat board in the west.
The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, as I understand it is to use every means within the power granted by the government to procure feed grains for eastern Canada and British Columbia at the lowest possible price. So we have in one region of Canada a government bureau which has been set up to promote the highest possible prices for feed grain, and in another region of Canada another government bureau which has been set up to promote the very lowest prices for feed grain.
Not only does this seem to involve an impossible situation, but consider, if you will, where it puts provinces such as Ontario, which is becoming a major producer of feed grains. In fact, Mr. Speaker, with respect to such grains as corn, oats and feed wheat, we in Ontario may soon find ourselves in an exporting position. Consider, if you will, where the carrying out of the principle of this bill would place the producers in Ontario.
There is no doubt that the only market the producers of Ontario feed grain will have is in the east. This is our traditional market, and this bill places us in this impossible position: we shall be selling feed grain to our traditional eastern market-which is and will be controlled, if the bill passes in its present form, by a government agency-in direct competition with the producers of feed grain in the west, who are protected by another government agency.
[Mr. Danforth.l
I think this should cause us to reflect on exactly what the government is doing. Also, Mr. Speaker, because of the government's subsidy on all western feed grains going into eastern Canada, we in Ontario have the additional handicap of having to pay freight on our grains going into eastern Canada in some instances six times as high as that paid with respect to feed grains coming from western Canada into eastern Canada.
If this bill is passed and such principles are set in motion-where a government agency controls the price of feed grains in an entire Canadian region and the avowed principle of such agency is to keep feed grains at the lowest possible price-in what position does it put those farmers in that region whose sole livelihood is derived from the production of feed grains? They would not be able to take advantage of any tremendous rise in the market. They would not be able to take advantage of the laws of supply and demand. Those farmers would be under direct government control in the prices they would be asked to accept.
When we look at the composition of the committee that is to administer this bill and look at the power that may or will be given to it, it is logical for us, on examining this bill, to look at the ultimate power that may be wielded by the committee as being the power we should consider. What do we find? First of all we find that this so called committee-consisting of five members, I believe-is appointed at the pleasure of the government. In other words the members are appointed for life, or until such time as they reach the age of retirement.
[DOT] (12:00 noon)
Now, the power which is granted to them is the power to buy, sell, transport or store feed grain to be used in eastern Canada and British Columbia. Mr. Speaker, these are the absolute powers which are set out in any provincial marketing scheme. The only difference, as far as I can see, is that the bill fails to provide two safeguards which the provinces always include; first, that any committee set up to regulate a marketing scheme should reach decisions only after advice has been given or recommendations heard from the groups who are affected by the scheme; and second, that individuals or groups of individuals who consider themselves the victims of an injustice have the right of appeal.
I am wondering also whether the absolute power granted to this committee is not an infringement of the authority of provincial
October 7, 1968

marketing boards. I say this because in Ontario there are already marketing boards set up to control the handling of grains used for feed. How are the provisions and regulations of provincial marketing boards to be reconciled with those introduced by the board contemplated under the bill before us? There could well be a direct conflict of interest because of the regional interests of both. I fail to see how such a problem could be resolved.
There is no doubt in my mind that a serious situation has existed and does exist in eastern Canada inasmuch as excessive profit has been taken from time to time with regard to feed grain. This is a situation which should be corrected, and I think it can be corrected. But I am doubtful whether the most direct or the most effective way of doing this is by means of the sweeping powers given to the board set up under the present bill. We are being asked now, in effect, to set up a cumbersome government bureau with full administrative powers over the eastern feed grain area.
During the war, when emergency powers were in being, it was possible to police all commodity prices, all wages, all salaries. This job was done by inspectors. Perhaps instead of setting up a cumbersome government bureau we could use the services of our present inspection staff in the Department of Agriculture. From time to time inspectors could call upon the distributors of feed grain in eastern Canada to ascertain the retail prices at which they were selling to farmers. This staff, on complaints by individuals or groups of individuals, could make inspections in order to determine whether an unjust profit was being derived.
There is no doubt in my mind that public opinion is the greatest police force we have when it comes to adjusting and correcting prices. We have seen evidence of this in the United States, where great corporations have increased their prices and later been forced to reduce them in the light of public opinion. We have seen the same thing happen in Canada. As a matter of fact, due to the activities of a group of irate housewives we have seen in the past few days how the prices of foodstuffs can be affected by direct action. So I imagine that such an agency as I propose would have the desired effect. It would be easier to administer, more direct in its effect and far less costly to the taxpayers of this country.

Canadian Livestock Feed Board
Again, one of our major problems in eastern Canada is the lack of adequate storage in places where storage is needed most. The present bill envisages the arrangement of suitable storage space in terminal elevators through arbitration and discussion so that feed grain can be moved in at an early date to take care of the normal requirements of feeders in eastern Canada.
In principle this is sound, but as far as Ontario is concerned it is unlikely to work by reason of the very nature of our harvesting program, which is carried out later than in the west. From time to time when we attempt to move our feed grain to the storage allocated in these terminal elevators we find there is no longer any room for it because the policy has always been to allocate space in terminal elevators on the first come first served basis. Thus we in the east find ourselves faced not only with an increased rate for storage but also with unjust demurrage rates on freight cars which are held up at terminals for weeks waiting to be unloaded.
How can the government provide storage? I think the desired results can be achieved in another way; by continuing the 25 per cent annual write-off on private or commercial storage. This would encourage grain companies to increase their storage facilities; it would also encourage private feeders and owners of small elevators to increase their storage capacity. It would be a golden opportunity for farm co-operatives to do the same so as to be in a position to buy feed grain at a reasonable price and have it on hand for distribution at a fair and even price throughout the feeding season.
That is what we need, a price which is fair and constant throughout the season so that feeders may be able to forecast their cost and decide in advance whether to increase or decrease their production. I say that if encouragement were given for the construction of private storage facilities, the problem of storage would be solved.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
The 25 per cent write-off would be a minimal expense to the government, and since the government envisages allocating at least $10 million to this new board for administrative purposes, and provision is made for more if it be needed, certainly this $10 million plus cost is far in excess of any diminished returns that could be expected as a result of the 25 per cent write-off. I ask the
8450	COMMONS
Canadian Livestock Feed Board government to give every consideration to this possibility in solving the problem we are considering today.
My third recommendation, and it is not a new one, is that the government consider reassessing the entire freight rate subsidy program. This is a complicated program. It is an expensive one. It was introduced as a wartime expedient. At this late date it may be impossible to do away with it, and I am not advocating that it be discontinued, but I ask the government to examine the matter once more to see if two objectives can be achieved.
The first objective is that it be administered more equitably between zones so that borderline cases do not suffer undue hardships and tremendous price fluctuations. The second objective is that it should not work such hardship regionally as it presently does in the case of Ontario. We in Ontario are penalized in two ways because of this government policy. The assistance on freight rates on western grain coming into and through Ontario depresses the price of Ontario feed grains to the extent of the freight assistance that is paid by the government. This assistance makes the feeders in Ontario extremely happy because they obtain cheaper grain, but it makes the producers of feed grain unhappy because it cuts severely into their profit margin.
That is the first handicap. The second handicap is that it places Ontario feed grain producers in an almost impossible position when competing with western feed grain growers in the eastern market. In some instances the freight rate on Ontario feed grains shipped from Toronto to Truro, Nova Scotia, is six times greater than on western grains shipped from the lakehead to the same destination.
For these reasons I plead with the minister that if in the reassessment he finds it impossible to alter the present freight rate assistance paid on western feed grains coming into eastern Canada, then every effort should be made to place Ontario feed grain producers in the same category as western producers. We are certainly entitled to be in the same competitive position as our brothers in the west with respect to the production and sale of our feed grains. Certainly the quality of our grains is competitive, and on that same subject the producers of western feed grains need make no apology for the quality of the grains they produce and ship into eastern Canada.
[Mr. Danforth.)
DEBATES	October 7. 1966
I see no justifiable reason why the freight rate assistance should not be made applicable to Ontario feed grains so that we may take full advantage of our markets in the east. It would provide the eastern feeders with the cheaper grain they are requesting. A reduction of $20 a ton on Ontario feed grain, by the application of the western freight rates, would make a tremendous difference in the price eastern feeders pay for grain. A government assisted freight rate for Ontario grains would solve another problem. It would increase the use of Canadian grains in eastern Canada as opposed to the importation of United States grain into that entire area.
Having dealt with this matter and put forward suggestions which I feel could correct the problem, correct it faster and to the satisfaction of all areas concerned, and correct it at much less expense to the taxpayers, I wish to conclude by dealing with one other principle. On behalf of the producers of feed grain in eastern Canada I am concerned where the future power will lie with respect to the granting of licences for the importation of feed grains. If my information is correct that power now lies with the western wheat board.
Is it contemplated that it will retain control over the importation of foreign grains, or will this power be delegated to the new board, if it is ever constituted? Will the two agencies operate as separate entities? Will they be subjected to double scrutiny? This is something which fills me with many misgivings, because very often the price of feed grain in Canada is set by the Chicago grain market, plus or minus any duties involved. If the price is set by the Chicago market and it becomes impossible to import feed grain, we could face an abnormal price situation due to the fact that grain could not move freely between countries.
These are some of the facts which I wished to place on record. This is not the simple bill that many of us were led to believe it would be. It is a most complicated bill. It grants tremendous powers to a government bureau. If I felt the bill would solve the problem, solve it quickly, solve it completely, and was the best approach, I would give it my unqualified support. But, Mr. Speaker, although I believe the government has sincerely tried to meet this problem I am convinced its approach is a costly one, a cumbersome one, and damage could be done to the feed grain industry in eastern Canada before such a cumbersome board as is contemplated could take the necessary action.
October 7, 1966

1 believe the direct approach of an inspection agency, with the write-off I have mentioned and an equitable adjustment of freight rates, would solve this major problem to the complete satisfaction of the feeders in eastern Canada, and eliminate the regional difficulty with which this bill does not cope. I still maintain that Ontario will find itself in an impossible position selling to a market that is under government control, and in direct competition with another government agency.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)

For several years, within my professional organization, I worked to see such a policy, such a measure implemented, as well as various policies about which I spoke during my election campaign, with regard to dairy farming and unemployment insurance.
But, in my opinion, the matter under consideration was the most important because as a farmer, and consequently as a buyer of feed grain from the western provinces, I suffered from those injustices in the handling of grain.
I suffered from the competition from feed producers because I was a director of a cooperative and I had, under the principles agreed to when the cooperative was created, to help those who had put their trust in me and buy grain accepted by the inspectors. Besides, at the same time, the feed producers had the chance to buy grain which had been rejected on the one hand, and which through another channel came into the hands of those who could compete with us. In his speech yesterday, the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois) dealt with a situation which can be applied to these grains-I followed his speech very closely and he was right to denounce the discrimination going on; I myself have been a victim of such discrimination.

Canadian Livestock. Feed Board
The grain had been rejected because it did not fully comply with the provisions of the act; in other words, instead of an 11 per cent content in proteins, the grain contained nonnutritive elements. Their protein content had been reduced to 8 or 9 per cent. An independent dealer had the opportunity to buy such grain of a somewhat lower quality and to mix it with some other products containing protein and thus increase the protein content of the grain, since the act authorizes the feed producer to add from 14 to 16 per cent of protein. Such tamperings are not too honest for you are still left with a percentage or a volume of non-digestible matter which cannot be digested by the animal, so that the value of this animal, when transformed into meat or milk, is not such that the buyer has his money's worth.
Mr. Speaker, fears expressed since yesterday are perhaps not too well founded. I have read the bill and it contains exactly what my professional association, the UCC, has been asking the government for years, and it is toward that end that we, in eastern Canada, have been working for so long at UCC's general conventions. This is why, after having read the bill, I find it meets requirements of the farmers. Sometimes, they may be justified in voicing apprehensions such as those which the previous speaker has just expressed but if the hon. member reads the text closely, his fears will be dismissed since the board may buy in any province, in the West, in the East or in Ontario, it does not matter.
Every aspect of the problem has been dealt with and I believe no one in this house would be justified in objecting to the bill.
Mr. Speaker, I was very happy to learn that the bill was being introduced just as I was coming into the house. I have only been here for a few days and it is precisely for this reason that I have been sent here. It is for this reason that I was elected on September 19. Contrary to what certain people who worked against me in my constituency may have thought, it is on the strength of my platform that I was elected, and I consider it to be of prime importance. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I will support it 100 per cent and I congratulate the hon. minister for his contribution in formulating this policy which is designed to help farmers in eastern Canada achieve their objectives.

Mr. Speaker, the fact that this bill, which finally
October 7, 1968

Canadian Livestock Feed Board has come before the house for second reading, has not received a great deal of public comment or debate of late reminds us all, I think, that it has been a matter of public concern for such a long time that perhaps there were even some who were under the impression that either it would never come up or that the bill had in some way already been passed but simply had not gone into effect.
As we were reminded in the house last evening by the minister, the intent of this bill was first brought before the house by the previous administration, when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) was minister of agriculture. It is very gratifying to see the present administration carrying on this good work and implementing the intent through this bill.
Needless to say, speaking as a maritimer, we have been under the greatest duress in obtaining feed grain over the past number of years due to the great fluctuations in price which have occurred. It is somewhat unnerving to be informed that recent events have taken place which lead one to wonder whether even with the implementation of this board we may be placing powers and placing our good faith in the government when we might not have the right to do so. I am referring to two things in particular which have occurred during the last month which have greatly affected maritime producers. One is with regard to the storage subsidy and the other is with regard to the drastic change in rates of freight assistance.
I am informed that about the first of September producers in the maritime region were notified that the storage subsidy which normally would go into effect on September 15 had been cancelled. In effect this could mean a loss of some $100,000 in Nova Scotia. Why such action should be taken when we are in the process of setting up new machinery to administer a very difficult and complicated area in our economic and productive life, I am not really sure.
The fact of the matter is that most of the producers already had committed their grain to storage, had counted on this subsidy, and then at the last moment it was withdrawn, the only explanation being that those economists whose wisdom seemed to be greater than that of the producers thought the subsidy had no effect in recent years; in fact they said it had not in any way decreased the cost of the feed to the producers themselves. I would argue rather, in a day and age of


increasing costs, that the subsidy may in fact have enabled some of the feed costs to have held the line.
An even more serious occurrence took place a few days ago, when notification was received on or about September 30 that on October 1 there would be a drastic change in freight assistance rates which could mean a possible loss of from $200,000 to $250,000 in the maritime area. No one is as yet quite sure whether this will mean a great increase in the rates. Meetings of feed representatives are being held today in the maritimes, and there will be meetings next Wednesday of representatives of the federation of agriculture to study this situation.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I mention all this only to indicate that it seems a strange thing that now, when we are contemplating these drastic changes in the distribution and cost of feed grain in eastern Canada and British Columbia, we should be doing such massive tinkering with laws and controls which we hope within the next six months will be greatly changed in themselves. I can only hope, as many in the maritimes do, that no more serious changes will be made until there has been a prolonged and exhaustive study made under and by the new board in order that the right assistance can be provided.
I am strongly convinced that one of the reasons the whole feeding and livestock program in eastern Canada has been at a serious disadvantage is that there has been only one agency at work looking after the feed program. That is the Canadian Wheat Board, which is concerned much more with the exporting and handling of wheat from western producers. When I speak today I speak not just on behalf of my own area or the province of Prince Edward Island, which in fact is producing a great deal of its own feed grain, particularly in the matter of beef raising; I think the minister mentioned 80 per cent but I feel the present figure is a little closer to 75 per cent. I am speaking for every maritime area including New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, most of which can only produce about 25 per cent to 40 per cent of their own feed grain.
These new policies are of great importance to agricultural producers in the Atlantic region, and they have been far too long in coming. There have been many resolutions initiated by a great number of farm organizations, and the word I have heard throughout
October 7, 1966

the maritimes is that this program must be implemented at the earliest practical time.
There are some fundamental questions that must be raised and there are some disquieting thoughts that come to mind in terms of the kind of policy that will eventually be spelled out in great detail and implemented by this new board. For instance, what are the dangers inherent in a program that may be produced by this board in directing or encouraging a program for vertical integration? What in fact is the size of the operation we are encouraging? Will the policy and program be directed toward encouraging the development of large combines, or is there some thought in the minds of those who have drafted this bill that this will be a great boon to those who are still convinced that the family farm has a role to play and a place in our country? These are things that will have to be spelled out. When will that be done? Will we just gather fragments and bits of information from this new board?
I hope that will not be the case, Mr. Speaker, but that the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Forestry, or the Minister of Finance or whoever is in essence the one who devises agricultural policy in terms of people-it is people that concern me-will be able to state at some early date some specific answers to these questions.
I am in agreement with the belief that in terms of many in the maritime region this will make operations that are now just barely viable, successful operations. If this is so, then many of these farming areas can be utilized to the fullest extent and many of the small farmers particularly can extend their herds and make full use of their farms, increasing their grass land.
I also agree with the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) who suggested that we are granting great powers to this board which will be composed of few people, three, four or five. I for one will be greatly interested to see what kind of people are appointed to these extremely important positions. There is perhaps a natural fear, because of past experience, that the kind of persons appointed will be the kind who can only examine cold statistics and who are intrigued by the economist and his slide rule, rather than by the practical experience and knowledge which exists now in various regions that make up this country.
Therefore what may be greatly important to us here in examining this bill will not only be the powers and composition of the board but the powers and the composition of the
Canadian Livestock Feed Board advisory committee, about which I will have more to say later. In this regard I am reminded very sadly of the many advisory committees that have been set up in similar circumstances which have turned out to be nothing more than rubber stamps, comprised of people who lose their local contacts three or four months after appointment.
That is not that kind of advisory committee I expect to see implemented or will press for when we come to the committee stage of our discussions. May I simply say, speaking as a maritimer and as a Prince Edward Islander, I feel in general terms that this bill offers great promise for the farm producers in our area.

We are wondering about it, because following the generosity of the Quebec government in this connection, prices keep rising ostensibly due to a shortage. But it must be admitted that it was a well managed shortage since the customers were finally looked after.
In the last two years, for instance, the price of seed oats has increased by $1.50 per hundredweight following a provincial grant of 50 cents per hundredweight for that class of grain.
Last winter, we all learned about the assistance given to cattle breeders by the federal government, jointly with the Quebec government. Such assistance was granted in designated areas following crop failures due to excessive rain in some cases and to drought, in others.
However, only cattle feed was subsidized and all hog breeders and poultry farmers had to pay the general price increase of 10 to 15 per cent on grain from the week when the subsidies were granted.

What part will the board play in such situations? Section 8 speaks of reasonable prices.
Will the minister tell us what he means by "reasonable" and how high the price of grain will have to go before it is considered unreasonable? Will there be price control in this field? I should like to quote a passage, Mr. Speaker, if I may be allowed to do so due to my lack of experience. Clause 16 reads:

What amount will the board be able to spend on this program? What scale will be used as a basis for deciding that a certain amount is adequate?
Will that amount be subject to credit restrictions, which have become current these days?
We can quote another statement, contained in the resolution introducing this bill, which reads as follows:
-and when authorized by the governor in council to enter into direct marketing operations in feed grain;
At this point, we ask ourselves: will some dealers be eliminated or will the new board serve as yet another middleman in already too long a list of intermediaries?
We note, as well, that the board will be authorized to made arrangements with a view to ensuring that livestock feeders have adequate feed supplies.
Will the board have men out on the road to find out what the requirements are?
Will the board provide for customers an information service like the one now provided by companies or responsible merchants?
Supposing that, for eastern Canada, the grain purchased before the close of the shipping season would represent only 25 per cent
October 7, 1966

of the expected consumption, would the board cover the risk of filling up the elevators of the areas concerned with, as sole guarantees, the consumption statistics of previous years?
Section 7 says that it shall be the duty of the board to make a continuing study of the requirements in eastern Canada and British Columbia. I hope that the word "study" here is only a word, because the time for study has been over long since and I suppose the minister will understand that now is the time for action.
In the same clause we read that the board will have to make recommendations to the minister and generally advise the government. I wonder whether the government will become very sensitive to recommendations made by its own employees it has chosen and whose names will be on the payroll?
If the government says it is ready to accept advice, how is it that the same government has always turned a deaf ear to representations made in that field by associations of grain and feed dealers, co-operatives and farm unions, as the Catholic Farmers Union?
All these questions make us believe that this board will play a very important and very delicate part. Everything will depend also on the powers given the board and the way these powers will be used.
I hope that all the farmers in the areas concerned with this new board will always receive the information to which they are entitled, and that the board will be really sure it is in a position to meet their needs and that we will have a truly improved policy, because the farmer has been the forgotten man for too long. During election period, Conservatives as well as Liberals have always taken pleasure in reminding him that he is the king of the farm. If he ever was king, we have proof that he has been dethroned for a long time, because as far as finance is concerned, his position proves that he is inferior to the majority of the workers in industry and he is far behind the majority of other professionals.
And in spite of his efforts, there is no way out for him as he finds himself caught between the price he is offered and the one he must accept for his products, and prices have gone up in the past 20 years, in some instances by 50 per cent in the case of grain and 100 per cent in the case of concentrates needed for livestock feeding.
For the last 15 years, the prices offered the farmer for eggs, chicken, turkey or other

Canadian Livestock Feed Board poultry have always been the same. The same thing can be said of meat such as beef, pork and other foodstuffs.
One must say he can hardly do something about it since he is dealing with perishable goods that he must deliver to the market as soon as they have reached the quality required by the consumer.
Such perishable products are none the less essential and farmers have proved that they know where their responsibilities lie.
I am convinced that it is precisely because they have fulfilled their duty too well that governments, regardless of who was in power, have ignored them.
The second reason why I think farmers are forgotten is because they have never honestly considered contributing to the election funds of the old line parties.
But the government realizes, I imagine, that it cannot rely indefinitely on the moral support of the farmers. The march on the Quebec Parliament organized by the farmers has proved that they can listen to electoral promises. But it has also proved that they can get together, between elections, to demand the passing of legislative amendments in their favour.
Therefore, we are anxious to see what this new board will do, and, if need be, we shall make further representations on behalf of this hardworking class which is not asking for charity but only for what is coming to them.

And from the other side of the house as well in at least one case. In rising to take part in this debate I wish to say at the outset that I do not categorically oppose this legislation. I think it has the prospect of considerable merit. In any case, the situation is such that one can afford to be optimistic, because I think there is hardly any field in what one might call agricultural economics where there is more room for improvement than the feed grain program for eastern feeders.
October 7, 1966

Canadian Livestock Feed Board
I do not want to be repetitious but I think it is well to recall the circumstances under which this policy was first brought into being. I can do no better than quote the minister's own words on this matter when speaking in this debate:
Freight assistance to teed grain and other grain products from the west to points of consumption in eastern Canada and in British Columbia was first started during the war, that is, in 1941.
Later he said:
The program served a double purpose: to expand the feed grain markets for the benefit of western grain producers and to enable farmers in eastern Canada and British Columbia to increase their cattle production.
The measure was brought into being during the war under special circumstances. We are now in the peculiar situation where an emergency program which was introduced under abnormal conditions has been continued long after its prime purpose has disappeared. It has been continued because of the side effects which the original program produced and which were possibly of relatively minor importance. This has left us in the intervening years with a very imperfect feed grain policy, and therefore I should like to say a few words of caution to the minister. This is my chief reason for rising at this time.
Ever since the introduction of this policy the two groups whose welfare seems to have been in the forefront of everybody's mind-I might include in this not only this and previous governments but also the Canadian Federation of Agriculture-have been the western feed producer and the eastern feeder.
There is a third group about whom I am greatly concerned but whose welfare seems to be considered as incidental. Nevertheless this program has had a great impact on them. I am referring to the producers of feed grain in eastern Canada, and I am specfically referring to the maritime provinces. This is of prime importance in the area from which I come. I am in complete agreement with those who wish to ensure that the commercial feeders of chickens or beef or the producers of hogs in the maritimes have a steady, reasonably priced and guaranteed supply of feed grain. But I have a further interest, and it is one which affects individual families even more because there are more farm families producing grain in Prince Edward Island than there are farm families using western feed grain.
This policy which was brought into effect 25 years ago has had a number of side effects over the years, many of which I think were


bad. This has placed the eastern producer of feed grain in a disadvantageous position. The reasons for this are rather subtle. They are small things, but in the aggregate they make it difficult for the producer to compete.
For example, back in the days when this program was introduced in the maritime provinces mechanization in agriculture had not progressed very far. In those days it was not possible for eastern farmers to produce feed grain in large quantities. Now there is at least that potential with full farm mechanization. If I remember my figures correctly, in 1944 there were something like 28,000 farm horses in Prince Edward Island, and by 1950 that number had dropped to 22,000. In 1960 it dropped further to 9,000 and a good share of these were either saddle horses, race horses or children's ponies. Now there are almost no horses used for the supply of farm power in the production of feed grain. Therefore the change in the type of farming in the maritimes has brought no corresponding change in a program which would make allowances for the increased potential in the production of feed grain in the maritime provinces.
In addition, there has been a lack of capital in the hands of potential maritime feed grain producers a chance to get high prices for risking any of the capital in their possession in the production of grain. The market has not been free in the sense of there being fluctuating prices which would give the local producers a chance to get high prices for their products in some years to make up for lower prices in other years.
In practice the situation has been that the costs to the feeder have fluctuated upward only when there was no local supply of grain. That was the only time the costs went up. The local producer therefore was in the situation of having nothing to sell when the price fluctuated upward. However, if the prices dropped down to the level of the subsidized price of imported feed grain he could not sell above that price, so that the importation of western feed grain to the Atlantic provinces tended to create a ceiling on the price the local producer could hope to obtain.
Another factor to be considered is that most or at least a great deal of the mixed feeds for the production of meat in the maritimes is supplied by local mills. Frequently they find it more convenient to have two or three carloads of western feed grain parked on their siding beside their mill rather than look in the local markets for relatively small lots of grain which would have to be bought

from individual producers and trucked to their mill. The result is that the local producer is always at a disadvantage. He is always suspected of wanting to sell grain which may have a higher moisture content and various other disadvantages in comparison with western feed grain, and he is never given the benefit of the doubt when he has superior grain to sell. All these factors taken together militate against the eastern producer being able to satisfactorily compete with the imported western feed grain.
What have been the effects of the feed grain policy on maritime agriculture over the years? I would not be so unfair as to ascribe the situation entirely to the policy which has been in effect. The facts of the matter are that although the world population is growing, and although many countries of the world are increasing their agricultural production, Canada is only doing so to a very limited degree.
[DOT] (1:00 p.m.)
In the ten years from 1953 to 1964, the average increase in the physical volume of agricultural production in Canada was at the rate of only 1.2 per cent per year. In the United States this increase was 1.8 per cent. The production of Prince Edward Island did not change. In New Brunswick the increase was only .7 of 1 per cent. The increase in Nova Scotia was 1.2 per cent. We like to think of ourselves as making great progress in agriculture in Canada. We like to think of ourselves as an advanced country agriculturally. Our effort in increasing the production of food over the last ten years compares very unfavourably with that of other countries, some of which we think of as being underdeveloped.
For example, in the same ten year period the average annual increase in agricultural production in Israel was 9.7 per cent. There is a whole, long list of countries ahead of Canada in so far as this increase is concerned. They are Mexico, Tanganyika, Yugoslavia, Venezuela, Brazil, Greece, Iran, the Argentine, Chile, Colombia, Pakistan, Tunisia, and then comes Canada. We are away down the list. In that rather sad picture the maritime provinces have been doing even worse than the rest of Canada.
In the five year period from 1956 to 1961, the latest year for which I have figures, the area of improved land in the maritimes declined from 2.3 million acres to 1.8 million acres. In other words, half a million acres of land went out of production in the maritime
Canadian Livestock Feed Board provinces during those five years. At the same time, in the three prairie provinces there was an increase of almost five million acres in the amount of improved land. I cite these figures to demonstrate the great potential in the maritime provinces, especially in Prince Edward Island, for an increase in production. The most obvious place in which this increase should occur, I think, is in the production of feed grain rather than importing so much from the west.
I am in full agreement with having a supply of western feed grain assured at reasonable prices. However, the west should not be looked upon as the source of all grain for eastern feeders. I believe that locally produced grain should be looked upon as the first source of supply and western grain as a subsidiary supply. We in the maritime provinces are in the ridiculous position of producing something like only half the meat we consume. There is a tremendous potential not only for bringing into production hundreds of thousands of acres in the maritime provinces which were once in production but also for increasing the production of those areas now in production.
I should like to quote briefly from a statement made by an official of the Acres Company, Mr. George E. Hunt. He said:
Can the maritime region produce more grain? I have here a chart which shows the effect of limestone on our highly acid sandy soil and just two levels of fertilization on oat yields. These aren't textbook figures but agronomist's data from actual work in the maritimes.
It has been demonstrated that we can have a five-fold increase in the maritimes through the use of fertilizer and lime. If we had even a twofold increase in our grain production on the land that is now producing grain, plus the bringing into production of some of the thousands of acres of land that once formed prosperous farms in the maritime provinces and are now dismal stretches of abandoned land growing up in scrub, there would be a great benefit not only to the feeders and producers of meat in the maritime provinces but to the whole economy of the area.
In closing, there are some recommendations I should like to make to the minister. I recommend that when the advisory board is constituted it have adequate representation of eastern Canadian feed grain growers. I should like to think that a more satisfactory way could be found to give some encouragement to farmers in the Atlantic provinces who would like to produce more feed grain than the mere subsidization of the import of
October 7, 1968

Canadian Livestock Feed Board feed grain. However, if even a small percentage of the large amount of money that is used for a rail subsidy could be transferred to the local grower of feed grain, that would have a very beneficial effect on the local economy and the user of feed grain in the Atlantic provinces who would have his problems met.
X should like to see even a little bit, say 10 per cent, of the subsidy that is now being applied to transfer feed grain from western Canada applied to a subsidy for the transportation of limestone and perhaps Saskatchewan potash to the Atlantic provinces. The world is now entering upon a period of tremendous increase in population and a corresponding increase in the demand for food. The population of the world last year was about 3.5 billion people. In 35 years it is going to be 7 billion people; that is the prediction, twice the population in only 35 years. It is estimated that food production can only keep up with the growth of population for perhaps 10 or 15 years, and then there is going to be a tremendous demand for food all over the world and therefore a demand for agricultural land and a demand for every means that can increase food production. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is one of the saddest commentaries that there are thousands of once prosperous one-family farms in the maritime provinces which have gone out of production, are growing up in scrub and are going to be needed for the production of food within the next 20 years. Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part briefly in the discussion on Bill C-218, an act to provide assistance to livestock feeders in eastern Canada and British Columbia.
This is a subject which has exercised the minds of those interested in agriculture for a long time. Thinking back across the years I can remember some of the debates which took place in the House regarding feed grain assistance and freight rate assistance. The problems which were faced then by the various segments of agriculture both in eastern and western Canada have not changed very greatly. The matters which were raised then are still of vital importance today and some of the arguments and representations being made at the present time are similar to those made years ago.
In this connection I have been checking the various manuscripts and briefs we have received in the past with reference to the establishment of a feed grain agency. I have before me a brief presented by the Federation of Agriculture dealing in considerable detail with the proposal to set up a feed grain agency and making a number of recommendations as to how it should be established and what its duties and responsibilities should be. I also have here a brief presented by the National Farmers Union to the government of Canada in which that organization also lays stress upon the necessity and importance of an agency such as is contemplated in the bill before us. In addition, I have a copy of the report of the standing committee on agriculture and colonization relating to the price of feed grain. On page 6 of this document we find this recommendation:
Your committee recommends the establishment of an agency, board or commission, hereinafter called "the agency", to be known as the Canadian Federal Grain Agency or by such other name as may be determined by parliament.
As I have indicated, there has for many years been a recognition of the need to see that prices both in eastern and western Canada should be fixed at reasonable rates and that feeders should be assured of adequate supplies of feed grain. When speaking on this subject some years ago I referred to the fact that in British Columbia feeders were required to pay almost four times the price at which feed grain was being moved in our sister province of Alberta. In Alberta, of course, grain can be moved from one farm to another without having to go through the Wheat Board and adhere to other regulations.
[Mr. Hees.l
The price in Alberta was about $20 a ton while in British Columbia it was approximately $70 a ton. I do not know what the present prices are.
An ironical aspect of the situation was that our people were forced to try to compete with products raised in Alberta and imported into British Columbia. This illustrates the impossible position in which growers in British Columbia were placed. So the whole question of feed grain prices was urgent then and is still a matter of urgency today.
The bill before us proposes to establish an agency to deal with such matters. I shall not go into the subject in detail today but I suggest that the task to be committed to this agency will not be an easy one to discharge. Sometimes we have taken the position that if and when an agency such as this is set up all our problems will be taken care of and it will be an easy matter to iron out the difficulties and remedy the inequities. But the proposed agency will not have an easy task before it. Too many difficulties are likely to arise in the administration of the program and in satisfying the legitimate interests of various regions. I agree with those who have suggested that in view of the wide powers to be conferred on this agency a tremendous responsibility rests upon its members to discharge their duties in a fair, equitable and satisfactory manner.
The duties are outlined in the bill. One of the most important aspects of this legislation is that a continuing study is to be made. With the passing of time circumstances may change. New problems may arise and some of the old ones may be solved. This subject will require continuing attention on the part of the agency so as to see to it that its responsibilities are discharged in a proper manner.
[DOT] (1:30 p.m.)
A great deal depends on the composition of the board, the persons who are to be appointed and their attitudes to the various problems. We also note the fact that an advisory committee is to be set up. In that connection I think I should refer to the suggestion made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture because this is one aspect that must receive careful consideration. At page 13 of the brief presented by the federation on February 23, 1965, it is stated:
Finally it is of the utmost importance that this agency which will be a state institution shall have advisory to it a committee composed of persons who are formally representative of organized farm groups in eastern Canada and British Columbia. Provision for effective consultation with and advice from producers is essential.
October 7, 196G
I have already referred to the fact that this is not going to be an easy task. Regional interests are involved. I have listened to the debate this morning with much interest because one of the factors has been the wide divergence of opinion that has arisen because of regional interests and concerns. These interests are legitimate. I am not saying they are not. While we in this group over the years have emphasized the absolute necessity of agricultural policies applicable right across the nation in comparable circumstances, we also recognize the fact that regions will be affected in different ways by the proposed agency and the application of particular policies.
For instance, there are regions within the prairie provinces which have different views on this matter simply because of the large geographical expanse of that whole area. This morning we heard hon. members speak of the difficulties of producers in Ontario, and just a few moments ago reference was made to the position of the maritime feed grain producers. There are even differences of opinion within the province of British Columbia due to the varied activities in that province embracing poultry, hog raising and beef production.
I mention these things just to point out that the setting up of the proposed board does not necessarily mean that everything will be automatically taken care of and that the problem will be easy to resolve. Its solution will require intensive and concentrated study. It will require a goodly measure of wisdom and discretion.
In general, while we give support to the concept of a feed grain agency we also join with those who have warned the government that because it is conferring such wide powers on this board it must see to it that the very best and most conscientious individuals are appointed to it and to the advisory committee. That is all I want to say at this stage, Mr. Speaker. I wish to give support to the principle involved and to warn the government that the problem merits great attention and consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that this bill has been introduced in an attempt to solve one of the most difficult problems in Canada, the equalization of opportunity for those people who make their living from the land. I believe we shall get off on the wrong foot right from the start unless we take a close look at the long-term planning of the Department of Agriculture.
Canadian Livestock Feed Board
It does not take great discernment to detect that there are a great many people in this country, particularly amongst agricultural experts, who have written off the family farm. According to them everything has to be bigger, everything has to be more efficient, and I mean "efficient" in quotation marks. In my opinion there is no efficiency in driving people from the soil. I think, and I believe I always shall, that the basis not only of a happy agricultural industry but of a happy nation must rest on a large and happy population based on its own land.
I sound this tocsin to the government and to the new board, which no doubt will be set up once we have tailored this bill to meet the ideas of some hon. members, that all of our agricultural policies must be based on the stability of the family farm. If the setting up of the proposed board will mean nothing more than the juggling of regional interests -I do not care how efficient they are in juggling them-if it means regional development and that regional development involves bigger and more "efficient" farms, then it will not solve the problem. It will not help to stabilize the living of a family that gets its living from the soil.
This bill envisages a multitude of regulations, and these may be arbitrary. The board is to regulate freight rates, subsidies and quotas, and the bill even refers to the possibility of importing large amounts of feed grain. The bill also contains a number of definitions and refers to assistance for people who raise livestock. Does this mean livestock raised on the family farm or does it mean the wholesale fattening of cattle in stockyards? There is a vast difference between the two, and I would like to go on record as saying that when it comes to a question of government subsidies and government regulations I do not think this type of operation should be developed to the detriment of the family farm.
The primary need is to protect the small producer who has no lobby and no money for lobbying, instituting lawsuits and exerting pressures. He is the man that this whole institution of parliament is designed to protect. He is the little man who has no other voice than that of his representatives in this chamber. I would suggest that it may and probably will be necessary to set quotas on the amount of subsidy which any group or individual may receive from the government.

I do not think it is right for us to sit here and say that out of the taxpayers' purse or

Canadian Livestock Feed Board out of the income of the small family farmers we should be subsidizing in any way these large or growing companies which are depriving the farmers of their legitimate birthright. As I think I said, the whole basis of this legislation should be to protect the interests of the small farmer who is very efficient in terms of humanity and in terms of the welfare of our nation in the real sense of the well-being and happiness involved in a healthy agricultural community.
There are, however, regional problems which I think should be looked at very carefully. In western Canada, particularly on the open prairies, the farmers depend very largely on one single product, wheat. The Canadian Wheat Board is faced with the problem of trying to stabilize agriculture in western Canada in the one product, wheat. But we have found in our experience that when we meddle with wheat it has a tremendous effect on all the other cereal products raised in Canada. If we sell the whole of our wheat crop abroad, it has a tremendous effect on the prices of grains in our own country.
When this new agency is set up I hope it will work very closely with the Canadian Wheat Board. I can only hope that great wisdom will be brought to bear by this agency on this problem and that the Canadian Wheat Board will not be anxious to denude Canada of cereal grains when these are very necessary for the production of livestock right here in our own country. I hope they will have the wisdom to see that such regulations as may be made with regard to cereal grains will not unduly antagonize the great republic to the south which has many of the same problems we have in respect of production, transportation, storage, and all the other difficulties with which this board will be faced. All these problems are shared by our great neighbour to the south. It may well be that with the best of intentions we may make regulations in this country regarding the feeding of livestock which will seriously affect the whole agricultural industry of this continent and perhaps of the whole world.
I hope also that this board will not be narrow and merely look at the distribution of feed grains. I hope they will take a statesmanlike world approach and try to tie in our policies with regard to the feeding of livestock in British Columbia, and particularly in Ontario and Quebec, with a world wide look at the whole situation in respect of livestock and good world relations. I hope they will put their whole weight and their whole planning

DEBATES	October 7, 1966
behind such things as the world food bank and take a realistic approach to world prices of food, be they cereal grains or feed grains, so that in the long term we do not destroy our good relations not only with the United States but with the whole world merely because we want a quick profit for our feed grain in Canada.
I know they will have these things in their minds but it is going to take, as the last speaker said, a great deal of wisdom on the part of the government to appoint the proper people to sit on this board, people who will look at the problem not only as a great Canadian problem but who will also have the statesmanship to try honestly to settle it in the best interests of all and, more than that, who will be able to co-operate as world citizens and help to develop policies which will help not only Canada itself but also our world relations.
It is stated that the whole problem will be investigated and I hope that means this agency will have wide enough powers to investigate policies starting with the farm right up to world markets so that there will be an agricultural policy which is not merely regional. I think this is going to take some sacrifice on everybody's part. Western Canada is quite willing to raise the grain, but it must also be realized that there are people in Ontario, Quebec, the maritimes and British Columbia who also raise grain and that it would be wrong to concentrate merely on the selling of excess grain from western Canada at any kind of bargain prices in these other areas unless a very close look is taken at the necessity of equality in the places which are importing this grain.
I also see difficulty in the proposal to set up regulations to protect the storage of grain. How is this going to affect the farmer himself? If the small farmer has to compete with a feed lot and the government in any shape or form is paying for the storage, this is a subsidy. I think we should take a look at the idea that perhaps up to a certain quota the farmer should be given some protection or be paid for storing his own grain on his own farm. I do not know the answer to this problem, but in some way he has to be protected against these large groups, whatever the cost in dollars and cents, because in the long haul it will be in the best interest of Canada.
In my opinion any agricultural policy in Canada must be directed at the family farm. When farms are big enough that they are no

longer considered to be family farms, I for one am not worried about them. They are big business, and big business always has been able to look after itself. If you are feeding 10,000 head of cattle you can buy in carload lots and you can distribute your labour force much more efficiently. I think the feature of the bill relating to the establishment of a co-ordinating and advisory board will meet with approval on all sides of the house. This is commendable because of the two-price system which exists in
8464	COMMONS
Canadian Livestock Feed Board the export and import of grain, and it is to be hoped that this advisory body will be able to create an atmosphere in which one price for feed grain in Canada will prevail.
We must always remember that on occasion subsidies are harmful to those areas they are intended to assist. So far as feed grain crops in Nova Scotia are concerned, there has been an increasing tendency on the part of farmers to rely on the importation of western feed grain. I think there is a controversial question involved in that suggestions have been made that Nova Scotia farmers are beginning to develop their own feed grain crops to meet their own needs. We welcome the establishment of this board but we do not want it to discriminate by its policies against the continuing development of feed grain farming in Nova Scotia. The western wheat growers and livestock raisers have expressed the fear that increased feed growing in the east coupled with subsidies will affect their industries adversely. It is interesting to note that, during the period from 1941 to 1961, in spite of feed grain assistance the number of cattle raised in Nova Scotia decreased from over 200,000 to 160,000. In 1964 the number decreased again. So it can be seen that a tremendously thriving livestock industry has not been developed in this area. The number of cattle raised in Nova Scotia in 1961 was 100,000 less than in 1921. While I appreciate the fears of the western wheat growers and livestock producers, with their wide open spaces, there has not been developed in the east, certainly in the maritimes and particularly in Nova Scotia, a cattle industry which could in any way compete. We are still importing cattle and we can hardly even suggest that we are self-sufficient so far as dairy products are concerned.
Perhaps the implementation of this new government policy will provide some stability in the livestock industry so that there will be an increase in production in the east. Government assistance is helpful, of course, to other types of producers. In our area an increasingly important poultry industry, has been developing, but this too has been in a transitional period, particularly in the Annapolis Valley. Farmers have lost some traditional markets. A pork industry has also been developed and the number of turkeys being

raised is on the increase. The assistance provided to these areas has had positive and productive results.

If this were done farmers who have suitable land could be self-sufficient feed grain producers. There are quite a few farmers in the area I come from who have properly drained and fertilized land and could produce feed grains sufficient for their own use and for sale in the Nova Scotian market. I believe the projections show that over 15 million bushels are expected to be required in the future, although at the moment we use only some 9 million bushels. Therefore there is a market and a need for this product.
In this connection the feed grain board could undoubtedly perform a useful function, but in order to encourage growth in this area and not rely completely on western feed grains there should be established a policy for the people who have not the land to continue to obtain feed grain imports, and for those who have the acreage to develop their own feed grains there should be a policy of encouragement which would be beneficial to eastern Canada and all segments of the country.
October 7. 1966

Apart from the question of having something more than a subsidy, which policy has a tendency to be negative, although overall in Nova Scotia there has been a definite positive effect, there should be an incentive for farmers to develop land that is fallow. There should be a sort of hybrid policy whereby the farmer could obtain a grant and invest in feed-drying kilns and equipment in order to process his own feed grain. This type of policy should be developed because the land is there and at the present time much of it could be developed in this way.
The question of storage facilities in the east is a very real problem. For instance, Saint John has not the proper facilities for loading grain and perhaps has not the positive qualities that are needed for a feed grain port. Neither Saint John nor Halifax has the storage facilities for feed grain which we in Nova Scotia need.
I would hope that the feed grain board would look at this problem in an advisory capacity and not concentrate solely on the buying and selling of feed grain. I would hope it would help in the development of storage facilities in the east, which are woefully inadequate at the moment for the ever-increasing market for feed grain. If the feed grain agency is only to buy and sell I think we have to watch, as previous speakers have mentioned, that it does not develop into just another agency that is concerned with costs and charges which are perhaps discriminatory in respect of local feed grain producers. There is room for improvement in this regard. A farmer can not buy directly from the Canadian Wheat Board, which has created many problems for him. Hopefully, the feed grain board will co-ordinate policy and eliminate some of the problems that exist at the present time. It is our hope that the board will be a watchdog over what happens from the time of the sale to the broker in Winnipeg to the time the feed grain ends up in the farmer's hands, because there is a very substantial difference in price between these two points.
However, Mr. Speaker, as a province which is concerned with feed grain more than any other Atlantic province we welcome the setting up of this board. We hope that the people appointed to the board will be truly representative of our area and will work to remove discrimination, keep costs down and co-ordinate policies rather than becoming involved in direct competition with the Canadian Wheat Board in the west. We do
Canadian Livestock Feed Board not want the anomaly of two boards in competition with one another.
In view of our past history and development we believe that the policy of paying subsidies should be directed more to providing grants to help the farmer develop his own feed grain resources. If we were also to develop our storage facilities in the east there would be a real improvement in our agricultural potential. I believe this is a matter the feed grain board should look into. In order that the debate may move on and the minister may close the debate on second reading, I do not intend to speak any longer. In general we in the east, and certainly those of us from the province of Nova Scotia, are in favour of the establishment of this feed grain board for which we have waited many, many years.

Mr. Speaker, I shall detain the house but briefly. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) has said that the establishment of this board is very encouraging to the farmers of Nova Scotia, and he certainly speaks accurately. There is no doubt that many of our farmers in particular lines of production simply could not have continued without the kind of assistance that has been afforded them over the last 25 or 26 years by the subsidy on the transportation of feed-stuffs. They are pleased to see that this subsidy is to be given a more permanent aspect by being put on a statutory basis.
I believe they are also pleased by the fact that the board will be given adequate powers to protect their interests as against anyone who might wish to intervene and make an unconscionable profit between the point where the grain leaves the producer in the western provinces and the point where it reaches the eastern feeder.
What I have to say, Mr. Speaker, goes beyond that question. The assistance that is provided is definitely of importance to agriculture as it now exists in our eastern provinces. Moreover, I think we would all agree that there is likely to be an increasing need for agricultural products as the population of this continent increases, and that it is a wise move to anticipate that demand for agricultural products.
Various speakers have mentioned some of the problems that the program, as it has been carried out has raised. For example, the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) mentioned the general exclusion of Ontario grown
8466	COMMONS
Canadian Livestock Feed Board corn, and the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings mentioned that there may have been times when the assistance on western grown feed grains has acted to some extent to discourage the growing of feed grains in the Atlantic provinces. He proposed certain very interesting approaches to the solution of that problem.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
I want to suggest to you, sir, that perhaps we should look further. I am wondering whether it would not be worth while to see if this money might not be more efficiently and perhaps more fairly expended by moving the point of assistance from the transportation link to that point at which the eastern producer brings his product, whether it be hogs, chickens or the like, to the market. If this were done he could find his feed wherever it is most economical to him, whether it be western feed grains, Ontario corn of his own produce. He could make that choice by his own lights and yet he would be encouraged and assisted in the production of the agricultural products that we need.
This would be a difficult approach to work out. DEBATES	October 7, 1966
with the members about the nature of the problem. Apart from certain partisan remarks made now and then, the debate actually dealt with the essential problem.

Yesterday a member of parliament-I think it was the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson)-spoke about the feed grain dilemma. It is a dilemma and has been one for many years, and until we have a national agricultural policy arrived at by agreement between the provinces and the federal government we will find ourselves in a difficult situation when we consider only one aspect of the problem, namely, the feed grain transportation subsidy to farmers in eastern Canada and in British Columbia.
Certainly the bill that we are now discussing has been in the minds of people for many years. As I said last night, in 1963, following the defeat of the then Conservative administration, there was a government notice of motion on routine proceedings and orders of the day in the name of the Minister of Agriculture proposing the creation of such an agency. A House of Commons committee then studied the problem and presented a report on March 22, 1965 proposing this legislation. The farm organizations of the country, as will be remembered by many hon. members, approved the principle of the legislation, and after first reading on June 30 the bill was widely distributed all across the country, so that everyone is familiar with its contents.
(Translation)
The fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that the establishment of this Canadian livestock feed board is a step forward in the development of a more rational agricultural policy for the country as a whole.
Nobody will dare claim that the passage or enactment of this bill will solve all problems. I believe we will a have a working instrument which will enable us, in the end, to make a more comprehensive study of several of the proposals advanced yesterday by hon. members.
Will there be any possibility of allowing Ontario corn growers and eastern feed growers to participate more efficiently in the program?
Must we promote a policy allowing eastern growers to grow their own grain? Must we try to change the feed transportation cost payment system, as suggested by two or three hon. members? All this remains a possibility. And I am pleased to note that members ask

themselves the same questions as the officers responsible for the administration of this act have asked themselves for the last three or four years. The reports prepared and the studies made raise the same type of problems that hon. members raised here, today and yesterday.
I am pleased to find also that we all have about the same line of thought. The principle of the bill has been endorsed by all hon. members, at least by all those who spoke; of course, there have been some genuine reservations here and there, and I hope I will have the pleasure of overcoming them when in committee.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
On the whole, there is no disagreement between the position of the government and that of all parties of the opposition on that bill. However, I feel bound to lay emphasis on two or three interventions, not only on the principle or the subject matter of the bill, but two or three interventions on particular problems which we may not have the opportunity to discuss in committee.
Two or three members have mentioned recent announcements by the feed grain agency or administration about the abolition of assistance to storage program in eastern Canada. We have paid in the past three years, one million two hundred thousand dollars for storage costs during a certain part of the year in warehouses of eastern Canada.
We have realized after perusing statistics that the payment of storage costs did not have the anticipated effect, namely it did not help to reduce cost fluctuations during wintertime and stocks accumulated in warehouses during autumn and winter were not so much different than those of previous years.
In our opinion, the special policy of subsidies involving $1.2 million intended for the payment of storage announced by the government has not had the effect that was expected. And we do not see why we should continue to ask parliament to vote such a large amount without being able to determine clearly who benefited.
On the other hand, since March, the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway are offering the brokers in the Atlantic provinces some arrangements for the transportation, over twelve months per annum, of such quantities of grain required by the farmers in three of the four maritime provinces. If we had maintained the payment of the storage costs in

There has also been a certain reduction in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland, in the payment of transportation costs. This problem is not new, but it has become more obvious since we allowed truck transportation, and since competition between railway and maritime transportation has increased.
